title: Proof is the New Proof
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey argues that AI has made ideas and even skills so cheap that demonstrated proof is now the only real differentiator on social platforms, and that higher education should take notice. He observes that application content, meaning case studies, live builds and show-and-tell, is winning reach because it shows real people getting real results. The listicle once served as proof of competence simply because few people took the time to make one, which is also how credentials like courses and degrees have worked. Once information and skills are no longer rare, that inference breaks down and volume alone no longer wins. He rewrites typical listicles in a proof-based form, such as mistakes made while growing a business or lessons from leading an AI transformation. His lesson for higher ed is that course completion is no longer proof, and that proof means learners actually doing the things the courses are meant to help them do.
points: Dempsey's core claim is that when AI makes ideas and ability abundant, the scarce signal is demonstrated proof of having done the work.
The listicle functioned as a credibility signal only because creating it was effortful, a logic he says mirrors how professors and degrees signal competence in higher education.
Application content such as scenarios, case study recaps and live builds is the format that now wins attention across platforms.
The shift means one carefully built post grounded in real experience beats a hundred generic posts, which reverses the older volume strategy.
For education the implication is to assess and credential what learners can actually do rather than whether they completed a course.
quotes: AI has made ideas and even ability so cheap that the only real differentiator left is proof. And if you don’t have proof, you aren’t going to get reach.
Simply: Real people, solving real problems, and getting real results that other real people need.
So whoever did actually take the time to create content like the listicle would, almost by default, be considered an expert. This was true whether they actually did the things or not.

We don’t necessarily know if the professor or degree holder can actually do anything, but we nevertheless infer from their proximity to some relatively rare skills and ideas that they have some level of credibility.

Time was, if you created 100 posts a week you were going to win on volume alone. Today, the person making one post using a refined post pattern based on proof of them actually doing the thing—that wins.
Course completion isn’t proof anymore. Proof is learners actually doing things that the courses are meant to help them do.
